To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. The ionizing flux of a “Born-Again” central star of a planetary nebula is not constant.
(1) The time-dependent recombination process of the “Born Again” CSPNe V605 Aql (Kerber et al. 2009) and V4334 Sagittarii (Kerber & Lechner 2009) is a very complex process.
(i) The recombination time scale is much shorter than the time scale for the change in the ionizing photon flux.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions:
    1. What is the recombination behavior of the “born-again shell” after the late helium flash of the CSPN?
    2. How does the ionization state of the nebula change over time?

the following questions: - What is the recombination time scale of planetary nebulae with respect to the ionizing photon production of the central star? - How can we describe the recombination of a planetary nebula in a time-dependent radiative-transfer model? - What are the consequences for the observable properties of “born- again” CSPNe?
the question of the ionization state of the nebula around V605 Aq and V4334 Sag after the late helium flash.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a time-dependent model is required.
the nebulae of the born-again CSPNe have to be treated in a time-dependent manner.
the ionization state of a CSPN is not only determined by its current radiation, but by its complete radiation history.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ionizing flux is so low that the recombination time scale of the nebulae becomes comparable to or even longer than the re-ignition time scale of the central star.
